title: Glowing Letter Tiles
story: In a phone word game you drag across letter tiles, and the trail glows on every tile you touch: green if the letters so far spell a word, amber if they could still grow into one, grey if no word starts that way. The dictionary holds tens of thousands of words, and the game adds new ones during a season.
task:
• constructor() creates an empty dictionary.
  • add(word) adds a word. Adding the same word twice is allowed and changes nothing.
  • isWord(letters) returns true if exactly this word was added.
  • isPrefix(letters) returns true if at least one added word starts with letters. A word counts as starting with itself.
Each method should take time proportional to the length of its argument, not to the size of the dictionary.
constraints: 1 ≤ length of every word and letters argument ≤ 20
Only lowercase letters a to z.

examples.explanation: "sta" is not a word, but both "star" and "start" begin with it, so the tile is amber. "start" was added, so its tile is green. No word begins with "stx", so that tile is grey.
"tea" is a word and a prefix of itself, so both calls return true. "te" is only the beginning of "tea", so it is a prefix but not a word.

hints: Write down "car", "cart" and "cat". All three share "ca", and two of them share "car". How could you store them so shared beginnings are written once?
Draw a tree where each edge is one letter. Every word is a path from the root, and words with the same beginning share the start of the path. Checking a prefix means following edges letter by letter.
After adding "cart", following c → a → r succeeds, but "car" was never added. What extra fact must a node remember for isWord?

Make each node a map from letter to child, plus a flag end that says a word stops at this node. add walks the letters, creating missing children, and sets end on the last node. Both queries walk the letters and return false at a missing child. If every letter is found, isPrefix returns true and isWord returns the last node's end.
bruteForce: Keep the words in a list and scan it for each query: O(n · L) for n words of length up to L. A hash set fixes isWord but not isPrefix, because a set only answers whether an exact string is present. A second set holding every prefix works, but it stores up to 20 prefixes for each word.

walkthrough: A trie (prefix tree) stores words letter by letter, sharing common beginnings. Each node stands for the letters read so far, its children are the possible next letters, and a flag says whether a word ends there.
• add "star" creates the path root → s → t → a → r and marks r as an end.
• add "start" walks the existing s, t, a and r nodes, adds a child t under r and marks it as an end.
• isWord "sta" walks s → t → a. The node exists but is not an end, so the result is false.
• isPrefix "sta" makes the same walk, which succeeds, so the result is true.
• isWord "start" walks to the second t, which is an end, so the result is true.
• isPrefix "stx" fails because there is no child x after s → t, so the result is false.
A common mistake is to leave out the end flag. Without it, "sta" counts as a word just because "star" passes through it.
solution.timeWhy: Every method follows one edge per letter of its argument, where L ≤ 20, no matter how many words are stored.
solution.spaceWhy: At most one node per letter added, and fewer when words share beginnings.
solution.takeaway: When you need to answer "does any stored word start with this?", store strings in a trie: one node per prefix, children keyed by the next character, and an end flag for complete words. Lookups cost the length of the query, not the size of the collection.
